key_insight: A finite-chord compressible scattering model can predict leading-edge noise reduction from perforated and porous inserts without fitting constants by using physically derived admittance models.
engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable aeroacoustic design of perforated or porous leading edges for turbulence-interaction noise control in realistic subsonic flow conditions.
method: Solve finite-chord scattering in compressible subsonic flow with arbitrary chordwise admittance, including wake, Kutta condition, and permeability-dependent edge singularities.
Derive perforate admittance from Rayleigh conductivity with corrections for plate thickness, aperture interaction, and grazing-flow blockage.
Model bulk porous inserts using measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia; represent finite span and array aperture in the far-field closure.
evidence_signal: The model matches perforate measurements to 2.5 dB rms over 84 comparisons and improves on the previously used unscaled impedance case (4.4 dB rms); two porous inserts are predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
watch_item: Measured narrow tonal peaks on perforated plates are not captured by the tested admittances, suggesting an additional convecting source mechanism not included in the frozen-gust framework.
paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
